refsect1.title: Dependencies
refsect1.para: Many settings in unit specification files refer to other units. They describe their mutual relationships and dependencies.
These references are formatted as YAML lists. A reference to just one other unit can be given as a single scalar value instead of a list with one value.

Other units get referenced by their filename, or name. It is not an error if the referenced unit is masked or not installed at all. This gets quietly ignored. The distribution's package manager presumably enforces programs' actual dependencies and requirements. vera's dependencies define the mutual relationship between different units when they are installed together:

listitem.para: This key is a list of other units that get automatically started when this unit gets started. A manual or an automatic start of this unit also automatically starts the required units. Stopping this unit automatically stops the required units if they are not required by any other started unit.
This is a one-way requirement. If unit A Requires: B, then: starting A automatically starts B (if it's installed and not masked); the opposite is not true.

note.para: Required dependencies are transitive. If unit A requires B and B requires C, then A also requires C.

listitem.para: This key is the one-way street in the other direction. If unit A is Required-By: B, then: starting B automatically starts A; the opposite is not true.
The Required-By: B dependency is logically equivalent to B specifying a Requires: A; this has the same result.

This key is equivalent to a required-by, but takes effect only when the unit is enabled. It typically refers to runlevels or targets, as described above. The only result from a vlad enable unit is that the unit's enabled keys get logically processed as required-by.

For example: a unit that's defined as enabled: system/graphical, then it gets enabled (by the enable command). The resulting required-by of the system/graphical has the following effect: switching, or starting, the system/graphical runlevel starts this unit (as part of the runlevel).

The order of multiple requires/required-by units is immaterial. Listing them in a particular order does not control their relative starting or stopping order. For example: unit A Requires: [B, C, D, E]. These four units get started by starting A. The actual order in which they get started gets defined by their before and after dependencies. Additionally, a requires-first dependency (see below) creates a before and after dependencies automatically.

These dependencies appear in both the Starting and Stopping keys. They control the starting and stopping order when multiple units get started or stopped together. When there are two or more units getting started or stopped at the same time:
vera checks each unit's Before and After dependencies.
This uses just the dependencies for the units that are getting started or stopped. Other listed befores and afters units get ignored.

note.para: Before and After dependencies are transitive. For example: A starts before B and B starts before C; D requires A and C. Starting D starts A before C. B does not get started (it's not required by D).

listitem.para: The Before and After dependencies get combined to derive their relative starting order, with respect to each other. For example, if A starts Before: B then: A gets started before B gets started; if A starts After: B then: A gets started after B gets started. The same applies to stopping units.

A Requires/Required-By dependency automatically creates the appropriate Before and After dependencies. A unit A that requires (or requires first, see below) B (directly by its Requires or the other one's Required-By) implies that A starts After B and stops Before B.
In the absence of direct or indirect ordering between two concurrent units, vera starts or stops them at the same time, in parallel.
The most common use cases should have mirror images of their starting and stopping dependencies. A Before starting dependency is typically a After stopping dependency, and vice versa.
It doesn't take many units to inadvertently create circular dependencies. vera randomly breaks circular dependencies after lodging a complaint.
A Requires-First dependency combines Requires together with Before and After dependencies. A Requires-First dependency, first, is equivalent to a Requires dependency, and additionally:

The transitive set of Requires and Requires-First dependencies get calculated. For the purposes of this calculation all Required-By dependencies are logically the same as specifying the equivalent Requires dependencies.
A second set of transitive dependencies get calculated from Requires-First dependencies, only.
Any units that are present in both sets get removed from the first set. The first set now contains only units that come from Requires and Required-By dependencies.
Every unit in the first set gets a Starting/After and a Stopping/Before dependency on each Requires-First unit.

The end result is that all Required-First units get started before any of the Requires units (and they get stopped after them). Otherwise, Required-First and Requires units get started concurrently, subject to any other before and after dependencies.

refsect2.title: Specifying hierarchical dependencies
refsect2.para: A dependency (Requires, Required-By, and all Before and Afters) can specify a hierarchical name, and it applies to all logical units in that hierarchy.
See for a description of unit hierarchies. For example:
This defines the dependency for networking/vpn, networking/interfaces and all other units in the networking hierarchy (and to networking itself, if this unit is defined).
